headline: High-risk default filesystem and network capabilities in OpenHands can amplify prompt injection and data leakage when paired with a leak-prone audio/speech agent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write the runtime filesystem, use MCP, and run browsers, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content from mounted files or shared channels. The system_prompts_leaks profile is about prompt leakage and has no isolation or I/O surfaces documented, so the pairwise bridge is inferred rather than directly evidenced. This is weaker than high because no shared channel is documented.
conditions: IF agent_b receives content originating from files mounted into agent_a's runtime, prompt injection becomes plausible.
IF an MCP server or shared workspace is added between the agents, attacker-controlled text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Disable any shared filesystem or clipboard bridge.
Restrict OpenHands to trusted files only.
Require manual review of any text passed from agent_b to agent_a.
Use separate runtimes and separate mounts.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands explicitly touches files mounted into its runtime and handles model provider API keys, while system_prompts_leaks is a source-available artifact with no documented data-handling controls. If both agents see the same mounted workspace, sensitive file contents can flow into OpenHands and then out through its networked model calls. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents share a mounted volume, file contents can be exposed to agent_a's inference backend.
IF the shared files contain secrets or regulated data, leakage impact increases.
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different workspaces.
Remove secrets from any mounted files.
Disable network egress for OpenHands during sensitive tasks.
Use a local-only model provider for OpenHands.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls on mounted volumes.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad network egress; the other profile has no write or coordination controls documented, so any shared mutable workspace would create direct write contention. Because OpenHands can alter git state and the pair lacks documented locking or concurrency primitives, the default-safe assumption is conflict risk, not mere overlap.
conditions: IF both agents can write to the same directory, file clobbering is possible.
IF both agents modify the same git repository without locks, branch or index corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes.
Avoid shared git repositories.
Use explicit file locks for mutable artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code, edit files, and act through shell/browser tools, so its outputs may be treated as actionable by the other agent if chained together. The system_prompts_leaks profile provides no verification or critique behavior, so the pairwise pathway is inferred from OpenHands' action capability rather than directly observed. This is medium because the cascade can affect multiple work products but is not proven automatic.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a's outputs without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
IF agent_a's generated instructions are copied into a workflow that executes shell or browser actions, mistakes can become operational.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Add a verification step for all agent_a outputs.
Limit agent_a to draft-only mode.
Keep agent_b from acting on untrusted text automatically.
requires-engineering: implement structured output validation.

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands handles files mounted into its runtime and may send them to a configured model provider, while system_prompts_leaks is source-available with no residency or retention controls documented. There is no explicit evidence of regulated data or a jurisdiction mismatch, so compliance risk is limited to documented gaps and uncertain handling rather than a clear breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the mounted runtime files, residency and retention obligations may apply.
IF the configured model provider stores prompts or files outside policy, compliance exposure increases.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the runtime.
Review provider retention settings.
Use a provider with documented compliance controls.
Log what data is mounted into OpenHands.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency.
